criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community piped drinking-water service access, connection modalities, affordability, and exclusion in low-income communities and informal settlements of Metro Manila.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it examines urban water privatization, regulatory governance, and institutional arrangements (Manila Water and Maynilad concessions and MWSS Regulatory Office oversight). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly analyzes concrete legal, regulatory, and administrative rules governing household water access: land-title and physical location eligibility rules for individual connections, two-month non-payment disconnection policies and anti-pilferage enforcement (National Water Crisis Act of 1995), MWSS Regulatory Office tariff and connection-fee rules (Resolutions No 05-006-CA and 07-023-CA; IRR # 2008-06), delegated collective payment/enforcement rules under bulk-metered micro networks, after-the-meter property/maintenance rules under clustered metering, and field manager discretion in withholding subsidized connection-fee rules.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary socio-legal empirical evidence from fieldwork in Metro Manila, including household surveys conducted by the author between August 2010 and May 2011 (including December 2010 surveys in an informal settlement), interviews with utility managers and community-based organization operators between October 2010 and May 2011, direct community observation, and regulatory document analysis. Per protocol safeguards, qualitative/mixed-methods socio-legal empirical studies are included even without pooled quantitative effect estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete access, connection, affordability, and exclusion outcomes, including denial of individual connections, connection fee burdens (PHP 15,000 to PHP 20,000 vs. under PHP 8,000 official fee) driving residents away from direct utility connections, ~50% tariff surcharges in micro networks, and actual vs. reported household connection coverage (300 connected out of ~800 households in Santa Ana).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (low-income households and informal settlements/communities in Metro Manila under the Manila Water and Maynilad concessions), rule-type exposures, access/affordability outcomes, and empirical case-study design (household surveys, interviews, observation, and documentary analysis) are all clearly identifiable, although exact total sample sizes for the surveys and interviews are not reported.

evidence_quotes.quote: This section examines two models that have been used to provide “more accessible” water connections to low-income communities in Manila – micro networks and clustered meters.

As a general rule, households with proper land titles and that are not situated in narrow alleyways may be eligible for individual connections; in the standard version, a meter is placed immediately outside the house.

Both concessionaires’ official policy is to cut off service after two months of non-payment. In reality, some degree of flexibility exists, in part because the concessionaires sometimes fail to register when those two months of delinquency have passed and because there may be room for negotiation between consumers and the local concessionaire staff.
This information is based on household surveys conducted by the author between August 2010 and May 2011, through which varying degrees of enforcement and billing became apparent.

This information is based on interviews conducted between November 2010 and May 2011. This community seemed to share the same issues with other micro network communities that I observed in Maynilad’s jurisdiction, but I chose to work in this settlement because the CBO and manager were particularly helpful in providing information.

Because the one-third/two-thirds scheme was not offered, and because the after-the-meter pipes are so long, those that are directly served by Manila Water paid connection fees up to double the official figure – ranging from PHP 15,000 to PHP 20,000 compared to just under PHP 8,000.
In reality, the micro network currently serves about 300 households, with the remainder using alternative sources.

raw_response.exposure: Privatized water concessionaires' non-revenue water (NRW) and service-access rules, including land-title and physical eligibility screening for individual connections, two-month non-payment disconnection policies, MWSS Regulatory Office tariff and connection-fee resolutions (Resolutions 05-006-CA and 07-023-CA; IRR # 2008-06), delegated collective billing/enforcement via bulk-metered micro networks, clustered-meter pipe responsibility rules, and field manager discretion over connection-fee cost-sharing
raw_response.outcome: Household piped water connection modality (individual connection, clustered meter, or CBO micro network), affordability (connection fees up to PHP 15,000–20,000 and micro-network tariff surcharges ~50% above utility rates), enforcement/disconnection risk, and exclusion/unserved household status
raw_response.population_and_sample: Low-income communities, informal settlements, and households in Metro Manila within the Manila Water and Maynilad concession areas (including case-study settlements using micro networks such as 'Santa Ana' and clustered-meter informal settlements; units of analysis: household, settlement/community, and utility concessionaire; exact survey/interview sample sizes not reported)
raw_response.rationale: Full-text socio-legal empirical study (Cheng 2013) examining how privatized water concessionaires' and regulators' rule-type mechanisms—land-title and physical eligibility requirements for individual connections, non-payment disconnection rules, bulk-meter/micro-network collective billing and unregulated tariff surcharges, clustered-meter connection-fee cost-sharing rules, and field manager discretion—shape household water connection access, affordability, and exclusion in Metro Manila's low-income communities. Based on primary household surveys (2010–2011), key informant interviews, field observation, and regulatory document analysis, the study satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1–c6) under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative / mixed-methods socio-legal empirical case study (household surveys, key informant interviews, field observation, and regulatory/documentary analysis)
